name: Koroshi
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Normally, nouns and adjectives are stressed on the last syllable (gar'den ‘neck’, ma'zan ‘big’). Even in the vocative, stress usually stays on the last syllable of nouns (ay dā'zan ‘hey woman!’), but occasionally – as in Persian – it moves to the first syllable (a'šī 'alamdār ‘he says: “Alamdar!”’). When the plural marker -(o)bār and the comparative suffix -ter are attached, they take on the word stress (bozo'bār ‘goats’, ġālī'bār ‘carpets’; mazan'ter ‘bigger’). In monosyllabic items, there is a tendency to move word stress to case suffixes, but in polysyllabic words it remains on the stem (bo'zay, bo'zā ‘goat (genitive, oblique)’; gar'denay, gar'denā ‘neck (genitive, oblique)’).
new_statements.citation: Nourzaei, Maryam, Carina Jahani, Erik Anonby & Abbas Ali Ahangar. 2015. Koroshi: A Corpus-based Grammatical Description. Studia Iranica Upsaliensia 13. Uppsala: Acta Universitatis Upsaliensis.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress on the final syllable of the (non-clitic) word: nouns and adjectives are stressed on the last syllable, and stress-bearing suffixes (plural -(o)bār, comparative -ter, attributive -ēn/-en/-īn, definite -ok/-ak) attract it; enclitics (copula, person-marking clitics, individuation =ī/=ē/=e) are unstressed, and case suffixes take stress only on monosyllabic stems. Verbs: past forms stressed on the final syllable of the stem (before the person clitic), non-past forms on the personal ending; the negation prefix na-, prohibitive ma- and subjunctive be- are always stressed and take the main word stress; complex predicates are stressed on the non-verbal element (plus the negation prefix if negated). A footnote states that stress placement 'is determined by higher-level phonological and discourse-related constraints rather than being a contrastive feature of word identity', so stress is not marked outside this section and the corpus.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; negated complex predicates are said to carry stress on both the non-verbal element and the negation prefix (za'rar 'nakanān ‘I should not make any loss’), p. 28.
new_statements.exceptions: Vocative occasionally shifts to the first syllable (as in Persian); monosyllabic stems tend to shift stress onto case suffixes; clitics unstressed; verbal prefixes na-/ma-/be- override the default; non-past verbs stress the personal ending. The authors add (p. 28): 'Phrase and sentence level stress and intonation, as well as syllable length, interact with word stress assignment. Consequently, the stress patterns described here are not absolute.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word excluding enclitics), described from a corpus of spoken narrative texts, not citation forms; the section also covers sentence intonation (falling in declaratives/wh-questions, rising in yes/no questions and preposed subordinate clauses). Data are from the northern (Fars/Shiraz) dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2015 grammar describes the northern dialect of Koroshi (Fars province, corpus gathered around Shiraz; the authors note a distinct southern dialect near Bandar Abbas, p. 25). Glottolog's hh.bib tags the work 'Northern Koroshi = Koroshi [ktl]'; Glottolog 5.1 has no separate dialect-level glottocode for Northern vs Southern Koroshi, so the statement is filed under koro1296 with the northern-dialect caveat.
